name: Software as a Medical Device
title: Software as a Medical Device
answer: Software as a Medical Device covers any software that a manufacturer intends to be used for a medical purpose, whether it runs on dedicated hardware, a general purpose computer, a phone or in the cloud. It includes products that diagnose, monitor, treat or drive clinical decisions, from automated image readers to dose calculators and closed loop insulin controllers. The category sits inside medical device regulation rather than general software law, which is what separates it from wellness apps and administrative tools. In practice the boundary is drawn by intended use, not by how clever the code is.

Governance, Compliance and Medical Device Security

sections.body: Software as a Medical Device covers any software that a manufacturer intends to be used for a medical purpose, whether it runs on dedicated hardware, a general purpose computer, a phone or in the cloud. It includes products that diagnose, monitor, treat or drive clinical decisions, from automated image readers to dose calculators and closed loop insulin controllers. The category sits inside medical device regulation rather than general software law, which is what separates it from wellness apps and administrative tools. In practice the boundary is drawn by intended use, not by how clever the code is.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These products run on a mix of hospital servers, vendor hosted cloud environments, mobile devices and embedded controllers attached to other equipment. Because many of them touch patient data or influence therapy, they usually sit inside a quality management system with design controls, version control, traceability and documented testing. Cybersecurity is part of the device itself, so manufacturers maintain threat models, patch pipelines and coordinated disclosure processes. Some run standalone, while others are components inside imaging suites, infusion pumps or monitoring systems.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work starts with a defined intended use and a risk analysis, then moves through requirements, architecture, verification and validation before any regulatory submission. Teams produce clinical evidence appropriate to the claim, which may be a retrospective study, a reader study or a prospective trial, and they keep the evidence tied to a frozen software version. After clearance or approval, changes are managed under a formal change control process, with some updates handled through predetermined change protocols and others requiring a new submission. Post market surveillance feeds complaints, malfunctions and real world performance back into the next release.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Oversight is layered. Regulators classify the device by risk, review the submission and attach conditions to the cleared or approved version, while standards bodies supply the consensus requirements for quality, risk and usability. Manufacturers carry reporting duties for adverse events and corrections, and they must show that privacy, security and clinical claims hold up under audit. Liability can follow the product, so documentation of design decisions, warnings and known limitations matters as much as the algorithm itself.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward faster, more continuous updating of software that is already in clinical use, with regulators building routes for planned modifications instead of treating every change as a new device. Expect more attention to transparency about training data, performance across patient subgroups and the behaviour of models after deployment. Security expectations will keep tightening as connected devices become targets, and post market data collection will carry more of the evidentiary weight. The open question is how review capacity keeps pace with the number of products reaching the market.
